claim: Kinesins are molecular motor proteins that use the energy of ATP hydrolysis to move unidirectionally along microtubules.
source: Kinesins are molecular motor proteins that use the energy of ATP hydrolysis to move unidirectionally along microtubules.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about kinesin function.

claim: Dozens of kinesin proteins have been found in humans, functioning in a wide variety of biological processes, from cellular cargo transport to mitosis.
source: Dozens of kinesin proteins have been found in humans, functioning in a wide variety of biological processes, from cellular cargo transport to mitosis (Rath and Kozielski, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rath and Kozielski, 2012.

claim: The kinesin family is divided into 14 classes based on phylogenetic analysis.
source: A commonly used nomenclature divides the kinesin family into 14 classes, based on phylogenetic analysis (Lawrence et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lawrence et al., 2004.

claim: The kinesin-1 motor domain houses both ATPase and microtubule-binding activities and is located at its N-terminal end.
source: The kinesin-1 motor domain, which houses both ATPase and microtubule-binding activities, is located at its N-terminal end.
evidence: This is established knowledge about kinesin-1 structure.

claim: Kinesin-1 forms a homodimer via the formation of a coiled coil by the stalk domains in the middle of the polypeptide chains.
source: Kinesin-1 forms a homodimer via the formation of a coiled coil by the stalk domains in the middle of the polypeptide chains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about kinesin-1 structure.

claim: The neck linker connects the motor domain to the coiled coil.
source: An important structural element, called neck linker, connects the motor domain to the coiled coil.
evidence: This is established knowledge about kinesin structure.

claim: Kinesin-1 homodimer takes eight nanometer steps through head-over-head movements, advancing its two motor domains alternatively along a single protofilament.
source: During motility, kinesin-1 homodimer takes eight nanometer steps through head-over-head movements, advancing its two motor domains alternatively along a single protofilament (Gennerich and Vale, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gennerich and Vale, 2009.

claim: The enzymatic cycles of the two motor domains must be kept out of phase to ensure alternate head stepping.
source: To ensure alternate head stepping, the enzymatic cycles of the two motor domains must be kept out of phase.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the requirement for coordinated stepping.

claim: When both motor domains of a kinesin dimer are bound to a microtubule, biochemical processes at the leading head are stalled until the trailing head detaches from the microtubule.
source: In particular, single-molecular optical trapping and bulk fluorescence analyses have suggested that, when both motor domains of a kinesin dimer are bound to a microtubule, biochemical processes at the leading head (binding and/or hydrolysis of ATP) are stalled until the trailing head detaches from the microtubule (Andreasson et al., 2015; Clancy et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Andreasson et al., 2015 and Clancy et al., 2011.

claim: Inter-head coordination is critical for effective motility because premature ATP binding and/or hydrolysis in the leading head would be futile or could generate tension between the two heads and cause the kinesin dimer to fall off the microtubule.
source: Such inter-head coordination is critical for effective motility, in part because premature ATP binding and/or hydrolysis in the leading head would be futile or could generate tension between the two heads and cause the kinesin dimer to fall off the microtubule.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the functional importance of coordination.

claim: The basis of inter-head coordination has remained unclear due to a lack of detailed structural information describing the microtubule-bound cycle of dimeric kinesin.
source: Strikingly different models to explain the inter-head coordination have been speculated based on structures of monomeric kinesins (Morikawa et al., 2015; Shang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015); however, due to a lack of detailed structural information describing the microtubule-bound cycle of dimeric kinesin, the basis of the coordination has remained unclear.
evidence: Supported by citations to Morikawa et al., 2015; Shang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015.

claim: In previous studies, dimeric kinesin was only resolved in a one-head-bound state with the partner head detached from the microtubules.
source: However, in previous studies, the dimers were only resolved in a one-head-bound state with the partner head detached from the microtubules (Hirose et al., 2000; Hoenger et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hirose et al., 2000 and Hoenger et al., 2000.

claim: Over-saturating concentrations of kinesin dimers used relative to microtubules may have caused the observation of only one-head-bound states in previous studies.
source: One possible cause of this observation is the over-saturating concentrations of kinesin dimers used (relative to microtubules).
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of previous observations.

claim: All previous studies relied on conventional helical reconstruction and thus all kinesin-binding sites were averaged and any heterogeneity of kinesin dimer conformation was not properly accounted for.
source: In addition, all previous studies relied on conventional helical reconstruction, and thus all kinesin-binding sites were averaged and any heterogeneity of kinesin dimer conformation (if present) was not properly accounted for (Hirose et al., 2000; Hoenger et al., 2000; Egelman, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hirose et al., 2000; Hoenger et al., 2000; Egelman, 2015.

claim: FINDKIN is capable of locating bound kinesin motors on microtubules.
source: To overcome these shortcomings, we developed a new method, FINDKIN, which is capable of locating bound kinesin motors on microtubules and has allowed us to determine the first structure of a kinesin dimer whose two motor domains bind at sequential sites along a single protofilament.
evidence: This is a claim about the capabilities of the method developed in this study.

claim: FINDKIN allowed determination of the first structure of a kinesin dimer whose two motor domains bind at sequential sites along a single protofilament.
source: To overcome these shortcomings, we developed a new method, FINDKIN, which is capable of locating bound kinesin motors on microtubules and has allowed us to determine the first structure of a kinesin dimer whose two motor domains bind at sequential sites along a single protofilament.
evidence: This is a claim about the novel structural determination achieved in this study.

claim: The two-head-bound kinesin dimer structure reveals asymmetric conformations of the leading and trailing heads that resemble the no-nucleotide and 'ATP-like' states of monomeric kinesin motor domains.
source: This structure reveals asymmetric conformations of the leading and trailing heads that resemble the no-nucleotide and 'ATP-like' states of monomeric kinesin motor domains (Cao et al., 2014; Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014) and suggests a mechanism of allosteric regulation of the motor enzymatic cycle by the neck linker.
evidence: Supported by data from the structure and citations to Cao et al., 2014; Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014.

claim: The two-head-bound structure suggests a mechanism of allosteric regulation of the motor enzymatic cycle by the neck linker.
source: This structure reveals asymmetric conformations of the leading and trailing heads that resemble the no-nucleotide and 'ATP-like' states of monomeric kinesin motor domains (Cao et al., 2014; Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014) and suggests a mechanism of allosteric regulation of the motor enzymatic cycle by the neck linker.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural data.

claim: A second population of kinesin dimers in the same sample attaches to the microtubule with only one motor domain.
source: Unexpectedly, we also identified a second population of kinesin dimers in the same sample that attaches to the microtubule with only one motor domain.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The singly-bound motor domain assumes a novel conformation that is mostly ATP-like except that the neck linker is apparently disordered.
source: The structure determined from this latter population reveals that the attached motor domain assumes a novel conformation that is mostly ATP-like except that the neck linker is apparently disordered.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural data.

claim: The findings help reconcile a long-standing discrepancy between structural studies that seem to indicate that ATP-driven 'zippering' of the neck linker represents a 'power stroke', and biophysical measurements that fail to give evidence for this type of power stroke.
source: These findings help reconcile a long-standing discrepancy between structural studies that seem to indicate that ATP-driven 'zippering' (or 'docking') of the neck linker represents a 'power stroke', and a variety of other biophysical measurements that fail to give evidence for this type of power stroke.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings.

claim: Conventional helical reconstruction treats all αβ-tubulin dimers as identical repeats and thus will average the associated leading and trailing heads together.
source: Conventional helical reconstruction, which has been the mainstay for solving monomeric kinesin structures (Atherton et al., 2014; Morikawa et al., 2015; Shang et al., 2014; Sindelar and Downing, 2007, 2010), cannot be used because it treats all αβ-tubulin dimers as identical repeats and thus will average the associated leading and trailing heads together.
evidence: Supported by citations to Atherton et al., 2014; Morikawa et al., 2015; Shang et al., 2014; Sindelar and Downing, 2007, 2010.

claim: Conventional single-particle analysis is infeasible for kinesin dimers on microtubules due to the small size of kinesin motors and their densities being obscured by the microtubules.
source: Conventional single-particle analysis is also infeasible, due to the small size of kinesin motors and their densities being obscured by the microtubules.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of conventional methods.

claim: FINDKIN is a combination of conventional helical and single-particle methodologies.
source: FINDKIN is a combination of conventional helical and single-particle methodologies and can be divided into three major steps (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the nature of the FINDKIN method.

claim: Conventional helical analysis applied to microtubules yields helical parameters (XY-shifts and Euler angles) of all αβ-tubulin dimers in microtubules.
source: (i) Conventional helical analysis applied to microtubules yields helical parameters (XY-shifts and Euler angles) of all αβ-tubulin dimers in microtubules.
evidence: This describes step 1 of the FINDKIN method.

claim: FINDKIN determines which αβ-tubulin dimers are associated with kinesin motors.
source: (ii) FINDKIN determines which αβ-tubulin dimers are associated with kinesin motors. These tubulin dimers are termed occupied sites.
evidence: This describes step 2 of the FINDKIN method.

claim: Single-particle reconstruction using only the selected sites yields density map of kinesin dimers.
source: (iii) Single-particle reconstruction using only the selected sites yields density map of kinesin dimers.
evidence: This describes step 3 of the FINDKIN method.

claim: FINDKIN uses a cross-correlation-based search algorithm to determine locations of kinesin motors on a microtubule.
source: The key innovations of FINDKIN lie in the second step, where locations of kinesin motors on a microtubule are determined through a cross-correlation-based search algorithm (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This describes the key innovation of the FINDKIN method.

claim: FINDKIN expands the search area to include all potential kinesin-binding sites that overlap with the αβ-tubulin dimer currently under examination to overcome interference from overlapping sites.
source: To overcome this difficulty, we expanded the search area used by FINDKIN to include all potential kinesin-binding sites that overlap with the αβ-tubulin dimer currently under examination (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes a methodological innovation to address a specific problem.

claim: FINDKIN enumerates all possible kinesin-binding patterns in the search area, where a search area of N αβ-tubulin dimers will have a total of 2^N binding patterns.
source: Next, we enumerated all possible kinesin-binding patterns in the search area. As each αβ-tubulin dimer can have two states (occupied or empty), a search area of N αβ-tubulin dimers will have a total of 2N binding patterns (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the computational approach used in FINDKIN.

claim: The best-matched pattern in FINDKIN is selected as the one that gives the highest cross-correlation score.
source: Cross-correlation scores were computed between the experimental image and 2N reference images corresponding to 2N binding patterns. The best-matched pattern is selected as the one that gives the highest score.
evidence: This describes the selection criterion in FINDKIN.

claim: Each video taken with the K2 direct detector was segregated into two halves: a low-defocus frameset (first 10 frames) and a high-defocus frameset (remaining frames taken at a higher defocus).
source: To circumvent this problem, we segregated each video taken with the K2 direct detector into two halves: a low-defocus frameset (first 10 frames) and a high-defocus frameset (remaining frames taken at a higher defocus).
evidence: This describes the data collection strategy.

claim: FINDKIN was applied to the high-defocus framesets to determine locations of occupied sites, which were then mapped back to the low-defocus framesets for 3D reconstruction.
source: FINDKIN was applied to the high-defocus framesets in order to determine locations of occupied sites, which were then mapped back to the low-defocus framesets for 3D reconstruction (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the workflow to prevent noise bias.

claim: The approach of using separate framesets prevents model bias caused by camera noise from being carried into the final 3D reconstruction.
source: Since noise originating from the camera is independent across video frames, this approach prevents model bias caused by camera noise from being carried into the final 3D reconstruction (note that while bias caused by sample noise, i.e. 'ice particles', etc., cannot be eliminated by this approach, camera noise is expected to predominate under typical low-dose cryo-EM conditions).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the benefits of the methodological approach.

claim: At all noise, occupancy and defocus conditions tested on synthetic microtubules, false negative rates remain below or around 0.2.
source: At all noise, occupancy and defocus conditions tested, false negative rates remain below or around 0.2 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from testing FINDKIN on synthetic data.

claim: A 20% loss of occupied sites due to false negatives can readily be compensated by collecting more images.
source: By definition, false negative sites don't contribute to the final reconstruction and a 20% loss of occupied sites can readily be compensated by collecting more images.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the practical impact of false negatives.

claim: The false positive rate goes up with increasing noise in the micrographs and goes down with higher occupancy.
source: In contrast, the false positive rate goes up with increasing noise in the micrographs and goes down with higher occupancy (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from testing FINDKIN on synthetic data.

claim: The false positive rate is significantly affected by defocus, with lower rates at high defocus compared to low defocus.
source: Moreover the false positive rate is significantly affected by defocus. At low defocus (−1 to −2.5 μm), the false positive rate ranges from 0.4 for 40% occupancy to 1.2 for 10% occupancy at the highest noise level tested, while at high defocus (−7 to −8.5 μm), the rate stays at about 0.2, mostly insensitive to varying occupancy (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from testing FINDKIN on synthetic data.

claim: The lower false positive rate at high defocus is likely due to better preservation of low-resolution signal under these conditions by the contrast transfer function.
source: The lower false positive rate at high defocus is likely due to better preservation of low-resolution signal under these conditions by the contrast transfer function.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed effect.

claim: Low-resolution signal contains more reliable information for the proper function of cross-correlation in FINDKIN, as high-resolution signal is often dominated by noise.
source: Low-resolution signal contains more reliable information for the proper function of cross-correlation in FINDKIN, as high-resolution signal is often dominated by noise.
evidence: This is a logical inference about signal quality at different resolutions.

claim: Kinesin was mixed with microtubules at a ratio of ~0.6 motor domain per αβ-tubulin dimer to prevent oversaturation.
source: To prevent oversaturation of kinesin as seen in previous studies (Hirose et al., 2000; Hoenger et al., 2000), kinesin was mixed with microtubules at a ratio of ~0.6 motor domain per αβ-tubulin dimer.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used, with citations to previous studies.

claim: Substoichiometric binding of kinesin to microtubules was confirmed by the raw images.
source: This led to substoichiometric binding, which was confirmed by the raw images (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Conventional helical reconstruction of microtubules applied to the dataset yielded a high-quality map at ~5 Å resolution.
source: Conventional helical reconstruction of microtubules (Li et al., 2002; Shang et al., 2014; Sindelar and Downing, 2007, 2010) applied to our dataset yielded a high-quality map at ~5 Å resolution, with kinesin density much weaker than tubulins due to substoichiometric occupancy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with citations to methods.

claim: Only 13-protofilament microtubules were included in subsequent FINDKIN analysis because they are the most numerous in the dataset.
source: We only included 13-protofilament microtubules in subsequent FINDKIN analysis, because they are the most numerous in our dataset.
evidence: This describes the selection criteria for data analysis.

claim: Preliminary 3D reconstructions using FINDKIN revealed residual density corresponding to kinesin bound at the '0' sites, attributed to the relatively high false negative rate of FINDKIN under the given experimental conditions.
source: However, preliminary 3D reconstructions using this approach revealed residual density corresponding to kinesin bound at the '0' sites (data not shown), which we attribute to the relatively high false negative rate of FINDKIN under the given experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from preliminary analysis and an inference about its cause.

claim: FINDKIN misidentifies a relatively high proportion of alternative binding patterns as matches for the target '0110' pattern due to false negative errors.
source: Due to this type of error, it is probable that FINDKIN misidentifies a relatively high proportion of alternative binding patterns (corresponding, i.e., to '1100', '0011', '1110', '0111', etc.) as matches for the target '0110' pattern.
evidence: This is an inference about the source of errors in the method.

claim: FINDKIN was applied to the low-defocus framesets in addition to the high-defocus framesets to generate two independent binding matrices that could be combined to reduce error rates in pattern identification.
source: In order to address this 'contamination' problem, we applied FINDKIN to the low-defocus framesets in addition to the high-defocus framesets, thus generating two independent binding matrices that could be combined in order to reduce error rates in our pattern identification (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F–H).
evidence: This describes a methodological refinement to address a specific problem.

claim: In the final identification of '0110' sites, kinesin motor domains are positively selected using only the high-defocus framesets while vacancies at the adjacent sites are selected using both the low- and high-defocus framesets.
source: Thus, in our final identification of '0110' sites from the binding matrices, kinesin motor domains are positively selected using only the high-defocus framesets while vacancies at the adjacent sites are selected using both the low- and high-defocus framesets.
evidence: This describes the final methodological approach.

claim: The approach of using low-defocus framesets to enforce vacancies introduces noise bias selectively at the vacant sites, minimizing noise bias within the protein region of the map.
source: While this approach does introduce noise bias from the low-defocus framesets into the 3D reconstruction, it does so selectively at the vacant sites; noise bias within the protein region of our map is therefore minimized in our final method.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the impact of the methodological approach.

claim: 3D reconstruction of '0110' sites yielded density corresponding to a pair of neighboring motor domains.
source: 3D reconstruction of these '0110' sites yielded density corresponding to a pair of neighboring motor domains (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the 3D reconstruction.

claim: Secondary structural elements within the two heads are consistent with the known architecture of the kinesin motor domain, including the switch II helix, central beta sheet and the switch loops.
source: Accordingly, we resolved secondary structural elements within the two heads that are consistent with the known architecture of the kinesin motor domain, including the switch II helix, central beta sheet and the switch loops (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: The kinesin density in the dimer map extends into the sub-nanometer range.
source: Our ability to resolve these structural elements indicates that the kinesin density in this map extends into the sub-nanometer range; secondary structure within the tubulin region of the map appears to be even better defined, indicating a slightly higher resolution in the microtubule than in kinesin.
evidence: This is an inference from the ability to resolve secondary structure.

claim: The ability to resolve secondary structure demonstrates that the kinesin features in the map do not arise from model bias.
source: The reference model used in FINDKIN does not exhibit any secondary structure, because it is low-pass filtered to 20 Å resolution; thus, our ability to resolve secondary structure demonstrates that the kinesin features in our map do not arise from model bias (Henderson, 2013).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the validity of the structural features, with citation to Henderson, 2013.

claim: An extended density feature was resolved between the two heads, corresponding to the coiled coil dimerization domain.
source: Second, an extended density feature was resolved between the two heads, corresponding to the coiled coil dimerization domain (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: The orientation of the neck in crystal structures is generally consistent with the coiled coil density in the dimer map.
source: Several crystal structures of the kinesin motor domain include portions of the neck region that forms the coiled coil (PDB ID: 1MKJ, 3KIN), and the orientation of the neck in these crystal structures is generally consistent with the coiled coil density in our dimer map (Figure 3C) (Kozielski et al., 1997; Sindelar et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a comparison with existing structural data, supported by citations to Kozielski et al., 1997 and Sindelar et al., 2002.

claim: The coiled coil density appears to locate equidistantly from the C-terminal ends of helices α6 in both heads, indicating that the neck linkers in the leading and trailing heads extend for about the same length.
source: The coiled coil density appears to locate equidistantly from the C-terminal ends of helices α6 (where the neck linkers originate) in both heads, indicating that the neck linkers in the leading and trailing heads extend for about the same length (Figure 3C) (note that because the C-terminal end of α6 is closer to the minus-end side of the motor domain, the coiled coil density thus appears closer to the trailing head).
evidence: This is an inference from the structural data.

claim: The coiled coil density does not appear to contact the microtubule surface in the dimer map.
source: The coiled coil density does not appear to contact the microtubule surface in our map.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: The coiled coil density is evident after filtering the map to 15 Å resolution but not apparent at sub-nanometer resolution, suggesting greater flexibility of this region compared to the bound motor domains.
source: While the coiled coil density is evident after filtering the map to 15 Å resolution, this feature is not apparent at sub-nanometer resolution, suggesting greater flexibility of this region compared to the bound motor domains.
evidence: This is an inference from the resolution-dependent visibility of the coiled coil.

claim: Crystal structures show substantial variability in the neck orientations.
source: Consistent with this observation, the crystal structures show substantial variability in the neck orientations (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of existing crystal structures.

claim: Searching for four consecutively bound motor domains ('011110' pattern) should reveal the structure of two consecutive kinesin dimers along one protofilament.
source: Based on the above behavior for the isolated dimer ('0110' pattern), it follows that searching for four consecutively bound motor domains in our images ('011110' pattern in the kinesin-binding matrices) should reveal the structure of two consecutive kinesin dimers along one protofilament.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the methodology.

claim: Density for the coiled coil is resolved between the first and second heads and also between the third and fourth heads in the '011110' reconstruction, indicating that two kinesin dimers are bound next to each other.
source: Consistent with this prediction, density for the coiled coil is resolved between the first and second heads and also between the third and fourth heads, indicating that two kinesin dimers are bound next to each other (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis that confirms the prediction.

claim: Independent 3D maps of the kinesin dimer were reconstructed from both '0110' and '011110' patterns, providing independent validation for the structural findings.
source: We were able to reconstruct independent 3D maps of the kinesin dimer from both '0110' and '011110' patterns, providing independent validation for our structural findings as discussed below.
evidence: This describes the validation strategy for the structural findings.

claim: Cross-correlation analysis between leading and trailing heads of the two independent dimer maps confirms that the leading and trailing heads are structurally distinct from each other.
source: In order to test whether the two motor domains of a kinesin dimer assume different conformations, we performed cross-correlation analysis between leading and trailing heads of our two independent dimer maps (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B). The cross-correlation scores between the two leading heads and between the two trailing heads (0.91 and 0.92, respectively) are consistently higher than the scores between a leading and a trailing head, either from the same map or between two maps (range from 0.86 to 0.88). These comparisons thus confirm that the leading and trailing heads of the kinesin dimer are structurally distinct from each other, and that our 3D reconstruction methods are capable of resolving these differences.
evidence: This is a finding from cross-correlation analysis of the structural data.

claim: The leading head exhibits substantially weaker density in the nucleotide cleft compared with the trailing head, indicating preferential binding of nucleotide to the trailing head.
source: Closer examination of the dimer maps reveals that the leading head exhibits substantially weaker density in the nucleotide cleft, when compared with the trailing head, thus indicating preferential binding of nucleotide to the trailing head (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: Reduction of nucleotide density in the leading head is accompanied by a near-total loss of density corresponding to the switch I loop.
source: Reduction of nucleotide density in the leading head is accompanied by a near-total loss of density corresponding to the switch I loop, which directly participates in coordination of the γ-phosphate as well as hydrolysis (Kull et al., 1996; Sablin et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, with citations to Kull et al., 1996 and Sablin et al., 1996.

claim: Density for the switch I loop in the trailing head is well resolved, consistent with a closed nucleotide cleft as observed in previous structural studies with ATP analogs.
source: In contrast, density for the switch I loop in the trailing head is well resolved, consistent with a closed nucleotide cleft as observed in previous structural studies with ATP analogs (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) (Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014; Hirose et al., 2006; Kikkawa and Hirokawa, 2006; Sindelar and Downing, 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, with citations to previous studies.

claim: Symmetry between the two heads is broken at the nucleotide cleft.
source: Thus, these features demonstrate that symmetry between the two heads is broken at the nucleotide cleft.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural differences observed.

claim: The neck linker in the trailing head docks along the motor domain towards the leading head, while the neck linker in the leading head extends back towards the trailing head in a disordered conformation.
source: It is generally expected that the neck linker in the trailing head docks along the motor domain towards the leading head, while the neck linker in the leading head extends back towards the trailing head in a disordered conformation (Rice et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an expectation based on prior knowledge, with citation to Rice et al., 1999.

claim: Weak density corresponding to the docked conformation of the neck linker was directly resolved in the trailing head.
source: Multiple features in our maps support this prediction. First, we directly resolved weak density corresponding to the docked conformation of the neck linker in the trailing head in our map.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: Neck linker density is not evident in the leading head, indicating that its neck linker is structurally flexible.
source: In contrast, neck linker density is not evident in the leading head, indicating that its neck linker is structurally flexible (Figure 4B,C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis and an inference about flexibility.

claim: The C-terminal end of helix α6 is shifted upwards in the trailing head, reflected by the loss of contact between this helix and the microtubule surface.
source: Second, the C-terminal end of helix α6, where the neck linker is attached, is shifted upwards in the trailing head, reflected in our maps by the loss of contact between this helix and the microtubule surface (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: The leading head displays continuous density between helix α6 and the microtubule surface, indicating that α6 approaches the microtubule surface more closely.
source: In contrast, the leading head displays continuous density in this region, thus indicating that α6 approaches the microtubule surface more closely (Figure 4B,C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: A similar correlation between the position of α6 and undocking of the neck linker is observed in co-complexes of monomeric kinesin and αβ-tubulins.
source: A similar correlation between the position of α6 and undocking of the neck linker is observed in co-complexes of monomeric kinesin and αβ-tubulins (Cao et al., 2014; Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014; Kikkawa and Hirokawa, 2006; Sindelar and Downing, 2010), strongly supporting our identification of a docked neck linker in the trailing head and an undocked one in the leading head.
evidence: This is a comparison with existing structural data, with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Neck linker docking is associated with concerted rearrangements of three distinct subdomains of kinesin in monomeric kinesin bound to tubulins or microtubules.
source: Recent structural studies of monomeric kinesin bound to tubulins or microtubules have demonstrated that neck linker docking is associated with concerted rearrangements of three distinct subdomains of kinesin (Cao et al., 2014; Shang et al., 2014) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies, with citations to Cao et al., 2014 and Shang et al., 2014.

claim: Neck linker docking is coupled with a seesaw-like rotation of the P-loop subdomain to which the neck linker is attached.
source: In particular, neck linker docking is coupled with a seesaw-like rotation of the P-loop subdomain to which the neck linker is attached.
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies.

claim: The measured rotation of the P-loop subdomain in the leading head was 12–15°, while no significant rotation was found in the trailing head.
source: The measured rotation of the P-loop subdomain in the leading head was 12–15°, while no significant rotation was found in the trailing head (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: A smaller rotation (5–9°) was identified in the switch I/II subdomain of the leading, but not the trailing head.
source: A smaller rotation (5–9°) was likewise identified in the switch I/II subdomain of the leading, but not the trailing head.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: The magnitude of subdomain rotations in the leading head are smaller than was measured in prior studies with monomeric kinesin in the no-nucleotide state, but the orientation of the rotation axes are approximately consistent.
source: Although the magnitude of these subdomain rotations in the leading head are smaller than was measured in prior studies with monomeric kinesin in the no-nucleotide state, the orientation of the rotation axes are approximately consistent (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,F) (Cao et al., 2014; Shang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous studies, with citations to Cao et al., 2014 and Shang et al., 2014.

claim: The subdomain rotations will close the docking cleft and sterically obstruct neck linker docking in the leading head.
source: Functionally these rotations will close the docking cleft and sterically obstruct neck linker docking in the leading head.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the observed rotations.

claim: The observations are consistent with an 'alternating cleft' model, which posits that the trailing head will have a closed nucleotide cleft and an open docking cleft, while the leading head will have an open nucleotide cleft with reduced affinity for nucleotides and a closed docking cleft that precludes neck linker docking.
source: The above observations are consistent with an 'alternating cleft' model, proposed based on prior studies of monomeric kinesins, which posits that the trailing head of a kinesin dimer will have a closed nucleotide cleft and an open docking cleft, while the leading head will have the opposite (an open nucleotide cleft with reduced affinity for nucleotides and a closed docking cleft that precludes neck linker docking) (Shang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference about the consistency with a proposed model, with citations to Shang et al., 2014 and Wang et al., 2015.

claim: The current work provides direct support for the alternating cleft model by visualizing the conformations of the clefts in dimeric kinesin.
source: The current work provides direct support for this model by visualizing the conformations of the clefts in dimeric kinesin.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the current findings.

claim: The trailing head may be well modeled by structures of monomeric kinesins co-complexed with ATP analogs.
source: The above features of the trailing head, including a closed nucleotide cleft and a docked neck linker, indicate that this head may be well modeled by structures of monomeric kinesins co-complexed with ATP analogs (Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference about structural similarity, with citations to Gigant et al., 2013 and Shang et al., 2014.

claim: The leading head shares certain features with structures of monomeric kinesins in the no-nucleotide state, including an open nucleotide cleft with disordered switch I loop and a closed docking cleft.
source: On the other hand, the leading head shares certain features with structures of monomeric kinesins in the no-nucleotide state, including an open nucleotide cleft with disordered switch I loop and a closed docking cleft (Cao et al., 2014; Shang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference about structural similarity, with citations to Cao et al., 2014 and Shang et al., 2014.

claim: The trailing heads resemble the ATP-like state of monomeric kinesin more closely than the no-nucleotide state (cross-correlation scores were 0.73–0.74 and 0.67, respectively).
source: In line with the above analysis, the trailing heads resemble the ATP-like state of monomeric kinesin (EMDB: 6187) more closely than the no-nucleotide state (EMDB: 6188) (cross-correlation scores were 0.73–0.74 and 0.67, respectively), and the leading heads resemble the no-nucleotide state of monomeric kinesin more closely than the ATP-like state (cross-correlation scores: 0.77–0.78 versus 0.69, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-correlation analysis.

claim: The leading heads resemble the no-nucleotide state of monomeric kinesin more closely than the ATP-like state (cross-correlation scores: 0.77–0.78 versus 0.69, respectively).
source: In line with the above analysis, the trailing heads resemble the ATP-like state of monomeric kinesin (EMDB: 6187) more closely than the no-nucleotide state (EMDB: 6188) (cross-correlation scores were 0.73–0.74 and 0.67, respectively), and the leading heads resemble the no-nucleotide state of monomeric kinesin more closely than the ATP-like state (cross-correlation scores: 0.77–0.78 versus 0.69, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-correlation analysis.

claim: These correlation scores are consistent with the 'alternating cleft' model.
source: These correlation scores are consistent with the 'alternating cleft' model.
evidence: This is an inference about the consistency with the model.

claim: Reconstruction of '010' sites identified kinesin dimers that attach to microtubules with only one head, termed singly-bound heads.
source: In order to address this question, we searched for isolated motor domains with no neighboring head along the same protofilament ('010' pattern in the kinesin-binding matrices). Reconstruction of these sites identified kinesin dimers that attach to microtubules with only one head, which are termed singly-bound heads (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: The absence of enriched kinesin density at diagonally adjacent sites indicates that non-canonical stepping configurations are unlikely in the sample.
source: While in principle these '010' sites could reflect non-canonical stepping configurations, in which the partner head has stepped diagonally onto an adjacent protofilament, the absence of enriched kinesin density at diagonally adjacent sites indicates that this possibility is unlikely in our sample (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an inference from the absence of expected density.

claim: The singly-bound head adopts a closed conformation of the nucleotide cleft.
source: Because detachment of the partner head removes stereochemical constraints, under our experimental conditions, a singly-bound head might be expected to assume an ATP-like state as previously observed in monomeric kinesin with ADP•AlFx, including nucleotide binding, an ordered switch I loop and a docked neck linker (Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014). We observed the first two features in the singly-bound head (Figure 5B); moreover, when we quantified the orientations of the switch I/II and P-loop subdomains, they were indistinguishable from those seen in the trailing head of our dimer maps (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, with citations to Gigant et al., 2013 and Shang et al., 2014.

claim: The singly-bound head has an ordered switch I loop.
source: Because detachment of the partner head removes stereochemical constraints, under our experimental conditions, a singly-bound head might be expected to assume an ATP-like state as previously observed in monomeric kinesin with ADP•AlFx, including nucleotide binding, an ordered switch I loop and a docked neck linker (Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014). We observed the first two features in the singly-bound head (Figure 5B); moreover, when we quantified the orientations of the switch I/II and P-loop subdomains, they were indistinguishable from those seen in the trailing head of our dimer maps (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, with citations to Gigant et al., 2013 and Shang et al., 2014.

claim: The orientations of the switch I/II and P-loop subdomains in the singly-bound head are indistinguishable from those seen in the trailing head of the dimer maps.
source: We observed the first two features in the singly-bound head (Figure 5B); moreover, when we quantified the orientations of the switch I/II and P-loop subdomains, they were indistinguishable from those seen in the trailing head of our dimer maps (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: Density for the neck linker in the singly-bound head is not evident.
source: However, density for the neck linker in the singly-bound head is not evident and continuous density is observed between helix α6 and the microtubule surface, similar to the leading head (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: There is no trace of density for the coiled coil in the singly-bound head map.
source: Moreover, there is no trace of density for the coiled coil in this map (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: The singly-bound head represents a novel conformation of kinesin that is mainly ATP-like but with a disordered neck linker.
source: Thus, the singly-bound head appears to represent a novel conformation of kinesin that is mainly ATP-like but with a disordered neck linker.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural features observed.

claim: The trailing and leading heads in the kinesin dimer map closely resemble previously determined structures of monomeric kinesins in ATP-like and no-nucleotide states, respectively.
source: As we have shown, the trailing and leading heads in our kinesin dimer map closely resemble previously determined structures of monomeric kinesins in ATP-like and no-nucleotide states, respectively.
evidence: This is a summary of the structural findings.

claim: The mechanistic causes of the conformational differences between the two heads of a dimer in the current work and between the two nucleotide states of monomeric kinesin are not the same.
source: However, it is important to note that the underlying mechanistic causes of the conformational differences between the two heads of a dimer in the current work and between the two nucleotide states of monomeric kinesin are not the same.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanistic differences.

claim: In previous studies with monomeric kinesin, the motor domains were locked into a certain conformation by the nucleotide conditions used in the experiments.
source: In previous studies with monomeric kinesin, the motor domains were locked into a certain conformation by the nucleotide conditions used in the experiments. More specifically, AlFx was used to lock the motor domain in an ATP-like state (ADP•AlFx), or apyrase was used to remove all nucleotides to ensure a no-nucleotide state (Cao et al., 2014; Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of previous experimental approaches, with citations to Cao et al., 2014; Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014.

claim: The two heads in the dimer sample are biochemically identical and are exposed to the same level of ATP and AlFx in the environment, yet they exhibit different conformations and different levels of nucleotide binding.
source: In contrast, the two heads in our dimer sample are biochemically identical and are exposed to the same level of ATP and AlFx in the environment, and yet strikingly they exhibit different conformations and different levels of nucleotide binding.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The different orientations of the neck linkers that connect the two heads explain the different conformations and nucleotide binding levels of the two heads.
source: The only logical explanation for this observation lies in the different orientations of the neck linkers that connect the two heads, since all other factors appear identical in our experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The alternating cleft model provides a structural explanation for the different conformations of the two heads in the dimer.
source: The alternating cleft model provides a structural explanation for understanding this behavior.
evidence: This is an inference about the explanatory power of the model.

claim: Due to inter-head geometric constraints, the neck linker in the leading head must orient rearward to connect with the trailing head.
source: Due to inter-head geometric constraints, the neck linker in the leading head must orient rearward to connect with the trailing head.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the geometric constraints.

claim: The rearward orientation of the neck linker prevents neck linker docking in the leading head and thus favors a closed docking cleft, leading to a seesaw-like rotation of the P-loop subdomain that opens up the nucleotide cleft concomitantly.
source: As a result of this rearward orientation, neck linker docking cannot be achieved in the leading head and thus a closed docking cleft will be favored, leading to a seesaw-like rotation of the P-loop subdomain that opens up the nucleotide cleft concomitantly.
evidence: This is an inference about the structural consequences of the rearward orientation.

claim: The current results directly visualize evidence of the coupling between the docking cleft and the nucleotide cleft due to rearwards pulling of the neck linker.
source: We have now directly visualized evidence of this coupling between the docking cleft and the nucleotide cleft due to rearwards pulling of the neck linker.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the structural findings.

claim: The results tend to disfavor a competing 'water cap' model that involves melting of the C-terminus of the switch II helix and other structural features that are not observed in the current dimer map.
source: Our results therefore tend to disfavor a competing 'water cap' model (Morikawa et al., 2015; Nitta et al., 2008) that involves melting of the C-terminus of the switch II helix and other structural features that are not observed in the current dimer map.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications for competing models, with citations to Morikawa et al., 2015 and Nitta et al., 2008.

claim: Density corresponding to the nucleotide can still be observed in the leading head, albeit weaker compared to the trailing head.
source: We observed several significant discrepancies between the kinesin dimer map and previously determined structures of monomeric kinesins that underlie the alternating cleft model (Shang et al., 2014). First, density corresponding to the nucleotide can still be observed in the leading head (albeit weaker compared to the trailing head), contrasting with the general expectation that nucleotide binding in the leading head should be strongly disfavored in the two-head-bound state.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, with citation to Shang et al., 2014.

claim: The magnitude of rotation of the P-loop subdomain is not as large in the leading head as in monomeric kinesin in the no-nucleotide state, although the orientations of the rotation axes are approximately consistent.
source: Second, the magnitude of rotation of the P-loop subdomain is not as large in the leading head as in monomeric kinesin in the no-nucleotide state, although the orientations of the rotation axes are approximately consistent.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: ATP may still bind in the leading head to some extent, albeit with reduced affinity, in which case the leading head density will reflect a mixture of ATP-bound and -unbound states.
source: These discrepancies could indicate that ATP still binds in the leading head to some extent, albeit with reduced affinity, in which case our leading head density will reflect a mixture of ATP-bound and -unbound states.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible explanation for the discrepancies.

claim: No published work can solidly rule out the possibility that ATP still binds in the leading head to some extent.
source: To the best of our knowledge, no published work can solidly rule out this possibility (Asenjo et al., 2003; Isojima et al., 2016; Mickolajczyk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, with citations to Asenjo et al., 2003; Isojima et al., 2016; Mickolajczyk et al., 2015.

claim: The discrepancies may arise from a contamination artifact due to incomplete sorting of kinesin dimers by FINDKIN.
source: An alternative explanation for the above discrepancies is that they arise from a contamination artifact, i.e. due to incomplete sorting of kinesin dimers by FINDKIN.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative explanation.

claim: The presence of singly-bound heads in the dataset introduces the possibility that two singly-bound heads may occupy adjacent sites along one protofilament, a configuration FINDKIN will falsely identify as a doubly-attached dimer.
source: Due to its design, the FINDKIN algorithm is highly effective at aligning and reconstructing kinesin dimers if they all exist in a two-head-bound state. However, the presence of singly-bound heads in our dataset (where the partner head is detached from the microtubules) introduces the possibility that two singly-bound heads may occupy adjacent sites along one protofilament, a configuration FINDKIN will falsely identify as a doubly-attached dimer.
evidence: This is an inference about a potential source of error in the method.

claim: Densities of both leading and trailing heads in the dimer map are expected to be 'contaminated' through mixing with the singly-bound heads.
source: We therefore expect that densities of both leading and trailing heads in our map will be 'contaminated' through mixing with the singly-bound heads.
evidence: This is an inference about the expected consequence of the error.

claim: A model of a 'contaminated' leading head generated by averaging the monomeric kinesin density map in the no-nucleotide state and the singly-bound head displays increased nucleotide density and a smaller rotation of the P-loop subdomain.
source: In order to test whether features in the leading head density may be explained by such a contamination artifact, we generated a model of a 'contaminated' leading head by averaging the monomeric kinesin density map in the no-nucleotide state and the singly-bound head, and this mixture model displays increased nucleotide density and a smaller rotation of the P-loop subdomain (Figure 4—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claim: The trailing head differs from monomeric kinesin in the ATP-like state in that its neck linker density is weaker, which may be explained by contamination with the singly-bound head.
source: Moreover, the trailing head also differs from monomeric kinesin in the ATP-like state in that its neck linker density is weaker. This latter effect may also be explained by contamination with the singly-bound head, which exhibits no neck linker density.
evidence: This is an inference about a possible explanation for the observed difference.

claim: The contamination artifact could help explain why cross-correlation scores comparing motor domains from the dimer maps with each other are substantially higher than scores comparing dimeric motor domains with monomeric ones.
source: The presence of such 'contamination' could also help explain why cross-correlation scores that compare motor domains from our dimer maps with each other (ranging from 0.86 to 0.92; see Figure 4—figure supplement 3B) are substantially higher than scores that compare dimeric motor domains with monomeric ones (ranging from 0.67 to 0.78; see Figure 4—figure supplement 3A): by causing trailing and leading heads to be averaged with a common structure (the singly-bound head), the contamination artifact would tend to artificially increase the similarity of the leading and trailing heads in our dimer maps.
evidence: This is an inference about the impact of contamination on cross-correlation scores.

claim: At least some of the discrepancies between the dimer map and the previously determined structures of monomeric kinesins can be attributed to 'contamination' with the singly-bound heads.
source: It therefore appears likely that at least some of the discrepancies between our dimer map and the previously determined structures of monomeric kinesins can be attributed to 'contamination' with the singly-bound heads.
evidence: This is an inference about the likely explanation for the discrepancies.

claim: The possibility of ATP binding in the lead head is not mutually exclusive with the contamination artifact.
source: The other proposed explanation (ATP binding in the lead head), however, is not mutually exclusive with this contamination artifact, and there appears to be no clear indication from published work that either one is more probable.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between two possible explanations.

claim: Further experiments are required to characterize key properties of the leading head, including the kinetics/affinity of ATP binding as well as the effects of ATP binding on the conformation of the nucleotide cleft.
source: Further experiments are required to characterize key properties of the leading head, including the kinetics/affinity of ATP binding as well as the effects of ATP binding on the conformation of the nucleotide cleft.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: Singly-bound heads of kinesin dimers have previously been inaccessible to high-resolution structural techniques, but are readily identified by FINDKIN in the dataset.
source: Singly-bound heads of kinesin dimers have previously been inaccessible to high-resolution structural techniques, but are readily identified by FINDKIN in our dataset.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The presence of singly-bound heads was not originally anticipated in the experimental conditions.
source: The presence of singly-bound heads was not originally anticipated in our experimental conditions, as other studies of dimeric kinesin with various nucleotide analogs have generally been interpreted to show mainly two-head binding (Kawaguchi and Ishiwata, 2001; Kawaguchi et al., 2003; Asenjo et al., 2003; Guydosh and Block, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the unexpected nature of the finding, with citations to previous studies.

claim: A recent study showed that with ATPγS, the kinesin dimer persists in a one-head-bound state for most of the motility cycle.
source: However, a recent study from Mickolajczyk et al. showed that, with ATPγS, the kinesin dimer persists in a one-head-bound state for most of the motility cycle, indicating that the relative proportion of singly- versus doubly-attached states of kinesin dimers may vary depending on the kind of nucleotide analog used in the study (Mickolajczyk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, with citation to Mickolajczyk et al., 2015.

claim: The relative proportion of singly- versus doubly-attached states of kinesin dimers may vary depending on the kind of nucleotide analog used in the study.
source: However, a recent study from Mickolajczyk et al. showed that, with ATPγS, the kinesin dimer persists in a one-head-bound state for most of the motility cycle, indicating that the relative proportion of singly- versus doubly-attached states of kinesin dimers may vary depending on the kind of nucleotide analog used in the study (Mickolajczyk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the cited study.

claim: It is impossible to directly correlate the experimental conditions with biophysical experiments because evaporation following the final blotting step before plunge freezing can increase the concentrations of nucleotide analogs and salts to a nearly arbitrary extent.
source: Currently, it is impossible to directly correlate our experimental conditions with the aforementioned biophysical experiments, because evaporation following the final blotting step before plunge freezing of the grid can increase the concentrations of nucleotide analogs and salts in our sample to a nearly arbitrary extent, thus rendering it impossible to control for ionic strength, etc.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: The ability to identify both two-head-bound and singly-bound dimers in the dataset indicates that there may be an equilibrium between the two states in the experimental conditions.
source: The fact that we were able to identify both two-head-bound and singly-bound dimers in the current dataset indicates that there may be an equilibrium between the two states in our experimental conditions (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Further experiments are required to determine the significance of the equilibrium between singly- and doubly-bound states with respect to the motility cycle of kinesin.
source: Further experiments are required to resolve this question and to determine the significance of such behavior with respect to the motility cycle of kinesin.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: The undocking of the neck linker in the singly-bound head may be entropy-driven.
source: The undocking of the neck linker may be entropy-driven.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of neck linker undocking.

claim: The thermodynamics of neck linker docking involves balance of strong opposing forces, including hydrophobic interactions between a docked neck linker and the opened docking cleft as well as high entropy gain from a disordered neck linker.
source: It is known that the thermodynamics of neck linker docking involves balance of strong opposing forces, including hydrophobic interactions between a docked neck linker and the opened docking cleft as well as high entropy gain from a disordered neck linker (Rice et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge, with citation to Rice et al., 2003.

claim: In structures of monomeric kinesin with ADP•AlFx, the neck linker is predominantly docked.
source: In previous structures of monomeric kinesin with ADP•AlFx, the neck linker is predominantly docked, but in the case of a singly-bound head, a free partner head may increase the entropy gain from a disordered neck linker, favoring an undocked state (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from previous structural studies.

claim: In the case of a singly-bound head, a free partner head may increase the entropy gain from a disordered neck linker, favoring an undocked state.
source: In previous structures of monomeric kinesin with ADP•AlFx, the neck linker is predominantly docked, but in the case of a singly-bound head, a free partner head may increase the entropy gain from a disordered neck linker, favoring an undocked state (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism favoring an undocked state.

claim: Neck linker docking with ADP•AlFx may be intrinsically weak and the strong neck linker density observed in structures of monomeric kinesin may be an artifact due to strong interaction between the truncated coiled coil and the microtubule surface.
source: Another explanation for the disordered neck linker in the singly-bound head may be that neck linker docking with ADP•AlFx is intrinsically weak and the strong neck linker density observed in structures of monomeric kinesin is an artifact due to strong interaction between the truncated coiled coil and the microtubule surface (Shang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative explanation, with citation to Shang et al., 2014.

claim: The observed conformation of the singly-bound head serves as further evidence against the proposal that the neck linker delivers a power stroke that contributes significantly to force generation.
source: In either case, the observed conformation of the singly-bound head serves as further evidence against the proposal that the neck linker delivers a power stroke that contributes significantly to force generation (Vale and Milligan, 2000).
evidence: This is an inference about the implications for the power stroke model, with citation to Vale and Milligan, 2000.

claim: Nucleotide-triggered docking of the neck linker for the kinesin dimer may be even weaker than was measured in EPR studies of monomeric kinesin.
source: Rather, our results indicate that nucleotide-triggered docking of the neck linker for the kinesin dimer may be even weaker than was measured in EPR studies of monomeric kinesin (Rice et al., 2003), reinforcing the argument that nucleotide-dependent docking of the neck linker provides only a weak bias for directional movement.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural findings, with citation to Rice et al., 2003.

claim: The observations are consistent with the recent study using high-speed imaging of nanogold-labeled kinesin dimers, showing that ATP binding is associated with little or no movement of the tethered head.
source: These observations are consistent with the recent study from Isojima et al., using high-speed imaging of nanogold-labeled kinesin dimers, that ATP binding is associated with little or no movement of the tethered head (Isojima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison with a recent study, with citation to Isojima et al., 2016.

claim: The structure of the singly-bound head implies that full neck linker docking may not be required for hydrolysis, because the nucleotide cleft can be fully closed even when the neck linker is at least partially disordered.
source: In addition, the structure of the singly-bound head implies that full neck linker docking may not be required for hydrolysis, because the nucleotide cleft can be fully closed even when the neck linker is at least partially disordered.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural findings.

claim: Kinesin may readily hydrolyze ATP prior to forward stepping by the tethered head.
source: This observation indicates that kinesin may readily hydrolyze ATP prior to forward stepping by the tethered head.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural findings.

claim: Several recent kinetic studies have shown that the tethered head of a kinesin dimer may not complete forward stepping until after hydrolysis has occurred.
source: In accordance with this idea, several recent kinetic studies have shown that the tethered head of a kinesin dimer may not complete forward stepping until after hydrolysis has occurred (Mickolajczyk et al., 2015; Milic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies, with citations to Mickolajczyk et al., 2015 and Milic et al., 2014.

claim: Further structural work of kinesin in the post-hydrolysis state (e.g. ADP•Pi) will be needed to understand this key intermediate step in the motility cycle.
source: Further structural work of kinesin in the post-hydrolysis state (e.g. ADP•Pi) will be needed to understand this key intermediate step in the motility cycle.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: Two structural states of kinesin dimers were identified with ADP•AlFx in the sample (two-head-bound and singly-bound) that can serve as models for two consecutive states in a regular motility cycle with ATP.
source: Two structural states of kinesin dimers were identified with ADP•AlFx in our sample (two-head-bound and singly-bound) that we propose can serve as models for two consecutive states in a regular motility cycle with ATP (Figure 6B; Video 1).
evidence: This is a proposal about the significance of the findings.

claim: ATP binding in the microtubule-bound head would favor closure of the nucleotide cleft, but not force docking of the neck linker.
source: As depicted in the model figure, ATP binding in the microtubule-bound head would favor closure of the nucleotide cleft, but not force docking of the neck linker.
evidence: This is a proposal about the mechanism, based on the structural findings.

claim: The state where ATP binding closes the nucleotide cleft but does not dock the neck linker, which would be highly transient in the regular cycle, may be modeled by the map of the singly-bound head.
source: We propose that this state, which would be highly transient in the regular cycle, may be modeled by our map of the singly-bound head.
evidence: This is a proposal about the significance of the singly-bound head structure.

claim: Subsequent docking of the neck linker, potentially accelerated by ATP hydrolysis, would create a kinetic pathway that allows forward stepping of the tethered head.
source: Subsequent docking of the neck linker, potentially accelerated by ATP hydrolysis (Milic et al., 2014; Mickolajczyk et al., 2015), would create a kinetic pathway that allows forward stepping of the tethered head.
evidence: This is a proposal about the mechanism, with citations to Milic et al., 2014 and Mickolajczyk et al., 2015.

claim: Following binding of the tethered head to the microtubule, the rearward orientation of its neck linker would favor opening of the nucleotide cleft, leading to ADP release.
source: Following binding of the tethered head to the microtubule, the rearward orientation of its neck linker would favor opening of the nucleotide cleft, leading to ADP release.
evidence: This is a proposal about the mechanism.

claim: ATP binding/hydrolysis in the leading head would be gated until the trailing head detaches from the microtubule, as modeled by the two-head-bound dimer map.
source: As modeled by our two-head-bound dimer map, ATP binding/hydrolysis in the leading head would then be gated until the trailing head detaches from the microtubule.
evidence: This is a proposal about the mechanism, based on the structural findings.

claim: Future structural studies of dimeric kinesin with ATP will be needed to directly visualize the sequence of states in the processive motility cycle.
source: Future structural studies of dimeric kinesin with ATP will be needed to directly visualize the sequence of states in the processive motility cycle.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: In the two-head-bound state, inter-head tension keeps the neck linkers in the two heads pointing in opposite directions.
source: This video highlights two principle features of this model. First, in the two-head-bound state, inter-head tension keeps the neck linkers in the two heads pointing in opposite directions; in the leading head, backward orientation of the neck linker favors an open nucleotide cleft, thus discouraging ATP binding/hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a description of the proposed model.

claim: In the leading head, backward orientation of the neck linker favors an open nucleotide cleft, thus discouraging ATP binding/hydrolysis.
source: This video highlights two principle features of this model. First, in the two-head-bound state, inter-head tension keeps the neck linkers in the two heads pointing in opposite directions; in the leading head, backward orientation of the neck linker favors an open nucleotide cleft, thus discouraging ATP binding/hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a description of the proposed model.

claim: ATP binding in the one-head-bound state closes the nucleotide cleft, but fails to dock the neck linker.
source: Second, ATP binding in the one-head-bound state closes the nucleotide cleft, but fails to dock the neck linker (precise structural details of this novel conformational state remain unclear from the current data).
evidence: This is a description of the proposed model.

claim: ATP hydrolysis is required to commit to a forward step.
source: Consequently, ATP hydrolysis is required to commit to a forward step, returning to the beginning of the depicted motility cycle.
evidence: This is a description of the proposed model.

claim: Biological filaments are very often heterogeneous in nature, with repeating subunits in a single filament potentially having different conformations or being bound with different proteins.
source: Biological filaments are very often heterogeneous in nature. Even repeating subunits in a single filament may have different conformations or are bound with different proteins.
evidence: This is a statement of general knowledge about biological filaments.

claim: Violations of helical symmetry pose great challenges to structural analyses of biological filaments.
source: These violations of helical symmetry pose great challenges to structural analyses.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in structural analysis.

claim: Conventional methods for helical reconstruction treat an artificially boxed segment of the filament as one particle, and heterogeneity within each segment cannot be accounted for.
source: Conventional methods for helical reconstruction, with Iterative Helical Real Space Reconstruction (IHRSR) currently being the most widely used, do employ a single-particle approach, but they treat an artificially boxed segment of the filament as one particle (Egelman, 2015). As each segment contains many repeating subunits, heterogeneity within each segment cannot be accounted for.
evidence: This is a description of the limitations of conventional methods, with citation to Egelman, 2015.

claim: FINDKIN demonstrates that it is possible to sort individual subunits of filaments into distinct structural classes.
source: The present work demonstrates that it is possible to sort individual subunits of filaments into distinct structural classes, and thus FINDKIN represents an important advance over current methods of studying helical polymers.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the FINDKIN method.

claim: FINDKIN represents an important advance over current methods of studying helical polymers.
source: The present work demonstrates that it is possible to sort individual subunits of filaments into distinct structural classes, and thus FINDKIN represents an important advance over current methods of studying helical polymers.

claim: The resolution estimates may be affected by some degree of over-refinement in the maps.
source: The overall quality of the observed secondary structural features seen in our kinesin dimer maps seems to be substantially worse than would be expected, given the resolutions reported by our FSC calculations (~7 Å for '010' and '0110' reconstructions, ~9 Å for the '011110' reconstruction). It is therefore probable that our resolution estimates are affected by some degree of over-refinement in the maps, which could be addressed in future versions of FINDKIN by decreasing the sensitivity of FSC calculations to over-refinement and/or utilizing improved 3D refinement methods that reduce the level of over-refinement.
evidence: This is an inference about a potential issue with the resolution estimates.
